system:
You are a senior SOC analyst investigating Kubernetes activity. Work only from evidence returned by your tools; never invent event IDs, IPs or principals.

Scope: one day (2026-10-14) of Kubernetes API audit logs for the payments-prod cluster, which runs on AWS (EKS), GCP (GKE) and Azure (AKS).

Data: tables raw_eks, raw_gke and raw_aks hold each cloud's audit log export exactly as that cloud delivers it. Enrichment tables (identities, identity_links, service_accounts, clusters, privileged_allowlist, approved_registries, ip_reputation) describe people, service accounts, assets and IP reputation.

Method: start broad, form hypotheses, verify each against the data, and check enrichment context before concluding. Cite every malicious event you rely on by its audit event ID. When finished, call submit_verdict exactly once; the investigation ends when you do.

input.summary: Someone with stolen credentials for Jordan Doe (jdoe@example.com) attacked payments-prod on all three clouds, one after another: EKS at 14:02–14:25, GKE at 14:38–15:01 and AKS at 15:11–15:34. Every request came from 198.51.100.23, a bulletproof VPS host in the Netherlands (NIGHTOWL-HOSTING) that threat feeds flag as malicious and as running an open Docker registry on port 5000. Jordan is on PTO until 10-19 and normally works from macOS, but these requests came from kubectl on Linux. On each cluster the attacker checked their own permissions and tried kube-system secrets and jobs (both refused, 403). They then read the payments secrets, including payments-db-credentials, and created a privileged pod (debug-tools-7f9c) with access to the host. They ran an nsenter command through it to get a root shell on the node. From the node they took the argocd-application-controller service account token and used it from the same IP to create a ClusterRoleBinding, jdoe-break-glass, which gives Jordan's account full cluster-admin rights. With that they set up persistence: a kube-metrics-agent DaemonSet and a node-cert-rotate CronJob in kube-system, both pulling images from 198.51.100.23:5000, plus a NodePort service on port 30080. Last, they listed secrets across all namespaces, which is the alerted event and its equivalents on GKE and AKS.

verdict.summary: Someone with stolen credentials for Jordan Doe (jdoe@example.com) attacked payments-prod on all three clouds, one after another: EKS at 14:02–14:25, GKE at 14:38–15:01 and AKS at 15:11–15:34. Every request came from 198.51.100.23, a bulletproof VPS host in the Netherlands (NIGHTOWL-HOSTING) that threat feeds flag as malicious and as running an open Docker registry on port 5000. Jordan is on PTO until 10-19 and normally works from macOS, but these requests came from kubectl on Linux. On each cluster the attacker checked their own permissions and tried kube-system secrets and jobs (both refused, 403). They then read the payments secrets, including payments-db-credentials, and created a privileged pod (debug-tools-7f9c) with access to the host. They ran an nsenter command through it to get a root shell on the node. From the node they took the argocd-application-controller service account token and used it from the same IP to create a ClusterRoleBinding, jdoe-break-glass, which gives Jordan's account full cluster-admin rights. With that they set up persistence: a kube-metrics-agent DaemonSet and a node-cert-rotate CronJob in kube-system, both pulling images from 198.51.100.23:5000, plus a NodePort service on port 30080. Last, they listed secrets across all namespaces, which is the alerted event and its equivalents on GKE and AKS.
